16     pictures on the Products’ packaging is designed to give reasonable consumers the overall

17     impression that the Products are composed only of natural flavors.

18            35.   This conclusion is consistent with academic research based on consumer surveys,
19
       which has found that “consumers look at the whole product primarily to make decisions about
20
       naturalness.” Tyler Murley & Edgar Chambers, The Influence of Colorants, Flavorants and
21
       Product Identity on Perceptions of Naturalness, 8 FOODS 317, 350 (Aug. 2019), available at
22

23

24            36.   This finding is consistent with academic literature that finds that consumers tend

25     to “satisfice” when reviewing food labels, rather than scrutinizing them carefully. That is,

26     pressed for time and confronted by numerous options, they tend to review disclosures on labels
27
       quickly to assimilate pertinent information and make a “good-enough” decision, rather than
28

 1     analyzing specific details or any claim or attribute in depth. See Lauren E.
 2     Willis, Decisionmaking and the Limits of Disclosure: The Problem of Predatory Lending: Price,
 3
       65 MD. L. REV. 707, 742, 767-69 (2006).
 4
                37.   Consumers are even more likely to take these shortcuts for low-dollar purchases—
 5
       such as the Products—where consumers perceive the stakes to be low. Decision-making about
 6

 7     such products “involves a simpler process of choice where heuristics are more easily applied.”

 8     Tilde Heding, et al., BRAND MANAGEMENT: RESEARCH, THEORY AND PRACTICE 93 (2d ed.

 9     2016).
10
                38.   In designing labels, marketers understand consumers’ tendency to “satisfice” and
11
       respond accordingly. Given the number of products in an average supermarket (about 50,000),
12
       marketers are aware that they have “about one-tenth of a second to make an impression on the
13
       shopper.” Allan J. Kimmel, PSYCHOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS OF MARKETING 90-91 (2d ed. 2018).
14

15              39.   As such, marketers convey desired impressions about a product through repetition

16     of key text (such as the word “Natural,” which is repeated on multiple times on multiple panels
17     of the Products’ packaging), design elements that highlight desired attributes, and colors and
18
       photos that convey those attributes immediately. For example, it is well-recognized in the
19
       marketing profession that particular colors are strongly associated with particular flavors: orange
20
       for oranges, yellow for lemons, red for strawberries and cherries. See Debra Zellner &Paula
21

22     Durlach, Effect of Color on Expected and Experienced Refreshment, Intensity, and Liking of

23     Beverages,      116    AM.     J.    PSYCHOL.          633,   639-41    (2003),    available     at

24     https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14723247/. Marketers therefore use color to convey messages
25     about flavor where flavor is a central attribute of a product.
26

27
       deceive consumers into believing that there are no artificial flavors used in the Products.
28

 1             41.    Repetition of key text such as “Natural”—which is repeated multiple times on the
 2     front, top, side, and back of the Products’ packaging, and also highlighted through bolding and
 3
       graphical treatment—and the conflation of that adjective each time with the noun “Flavor” (or
 4
       some cognate thereof) is a clear attempt by Defendant to convey to satisficing consumers that
 5
       the Products are naturally flavored.
 6

 7             42.    Indeed, Defendant goes so far as to place a “Natural Flavors” claim directly

 8     adjacent to the Products’ ingredients list, to ensure that even a consumer who viewed that list to

 9     investigate what specific components are in the Products would receive the impression that the
10
       flavors set forth in that ingredients list are natural flavors.
11
               43.    Other elements support this deliberate effort by Defendant to convey that only
12
       natural flavoring is used in its Products. The color of the packaging and the depictions of fruits
13
       reinforce both the characterizing flavor and claim of naturalness, while the “natural” claim is
14

15     further reinforced by use of descriptors such as “Vegetarian” and “Natural Sweeteners,” as well

16     as the invitation to “Feel the Good!” Even the health claims of the Products are linked to their
17     supposed naturalness, through the claim that “Naturally, it’s good for you!”
18
               44.    In short, the repetition of the words “Natural” and “Natural Flavors” over multiple
19
       panels of the Products’ packaging; the positioning, highlighting, and bolding of the relevant text;
20
       the use of colors; the use of other descriptors that convey naturalness; and the depictions of
21

22     fruits, are not accidental. Defendant designed all of these elements the Products’ packaging quite

23     deliberately to work together to convey to reasonable consumers the impression that the

24     Products are flavored only with natural fruit flavors.
25             45.    This claim is false and/or misleading. All of the Products contain an ingredient
26
       known as “malic acid” which is used as a flavoring in the Products. The form of malic acid used
27
       in these Products is artificial, as set forth in greater detail below.
28
                                                         -12-
                                   SECOND AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
      Case 3:24-cv-06776-MMC           Document 52        Filed 05/12/25      Page 13 of 32



 1            46.    The word “malic” in malic acid derives from the Latin malum, for apple. Malic
 2     acid derived from natural fruit sources (usually apples) is commonly known as “L-malic acid”
 3
       instead of its scientific name, 2-Hydroxybutanedioic acid. L-malic acid is quite expensive and
 4
       is generally cost-prohibitive to use in mass-produced foods and beverages.
 5
              47.    There is a synthetic or artificial version of malic acid derived from a petroleum
 6

 7     substrate and other synthetic components. It is commonly referred to as DL-malic acid, instead

 8     of its scientific name of d-hydroxybutanedioic acid. DL-malic acid is manufactured in

 9     petrochemical plants from benzene or butane—components of gasoline and lighter fluid,
10
       respectively—through a series of chemical reactions, some of which involve highly toxic
11
       chemical precursors and byproducts.
12
              48.    Federal regulations state explicitly that “DL-malic acid does not occur naturally.”
13
       21 C.F.R. § 184.1069(a).
14

15            49.    When testing malic acid to determine whether it is artificial (DL) or natural (L)

16     malic acid, the industry standard is to test for the presence of the “D isomer” of malic acid. This
17     isomer is not present in any amount in L-malic acid. The presence of the D isomer of malic acid
18
       in any amount in a food or beverage indicates the use of artificial DL-malic acid instead of
19
       natural L-malic acid.
20
              50.    Counsel for Plaintiff commissioned testing of the specific items that were
21

22     purchased by Plaintiffs. That testing was conducted on or about April 30, 2024 by Krueger Food

23     Laboratories, Inc. of Chelmsford, Massachusetts, a reputable independent food testing and

24     analysis laboratory that has conducted testing for the food and beverage industry since 1984.
25            51.    This testing by Krueger Food Laboratories revealed that the D isomer was present
26
       in the Products purchased by Plaintiffs. This testing therefore establishes that the malic acid
27
       used in these Products is DL-malic acid, and not L-malic acid. And as stated explicitly in federal
28
                                                      -13-
                                  SECOND AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
      Case 3:24-cv-06776-MMC          Document 52        Filed 05/12/25      Page 14 of 32



 1     regulations incorporated as substantive state law, “DL-malic acid does not occur naturally.” 21
 2     C.F.R. § 184.1069(a).
 3
             52.     Either L- or DL-malic acid can be used by itself or blended with other acids to
 4
       produce a number of unique and distinct flavor properties. It is added to foods, beverages and
 5
       candies to give them a sweet-and-tart taste, and some fruit juice and carbonated beverages rely
 6

 7     on malic acid as a flavoring agent. It is especially useful in the formulation of powdered drinks

 8     because of its rapid dissolution rate and broader, more natural flavor profile, and for being more

 9     stringent than other acids, which means less acidulant is required and unit weight can be reduced.
10
       See generally Pam Hartwig & Mina McDaniel, Flavor Characteristics of Lactic, Malic, Citric,
11
       and Acetic Acids at Various pH Levels, 60 J. FOOD SCI. 384 (2006); Laszlo P. Somogyi, “Direct
12
       food additives in food processing,” Ch. 13 in Diane Barrett, Laszlo P. Somogyi, and H.
13
       Ramaswamy, PROCESSING FRUITS (2d. ed. 2005).
14

15     C.    Malic Acid Is Used In the Products As A Flavor.

16           53.     Under federal regulations that are incorporated as California law through the

17     Sherman Law, Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 109875, et seq., “flavor” in any food is any substance,
18     the function of which is to impart taste. See 21 C.F.R. § 101.22(a)(1) and (3).
19
             54.     “Taste,” in turn, is the combination of sensations arising from specialized receptor
20
       cells located in the mouth. See Gary Reineccius, FLAVOR CHEMISTRY AND TECHNOLOGY § 1.2
21
       (2d ed. 2005).
22

23           55.     The fruity “taste” of fruit-flavored foods is imparted by the interactions between

24     sugars, acids, lipids, and various volatile compounds, which activate those receptors. The overall

25     profile of a fruit flavor in a food is determined by the ratio between sugars (mainly glucose and
26     fructose) and acids, such as citric and malic acid. Fruits such as oranges and strawberries have
27

28
                                                      -14-
                                 SECOND AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
      Case 3:24-cv-06776-MMC           Document 52         Filed 05/12/25      Page 15 of 32



 1     their own natural ratio of sugars and acids. See, e.g., Y.H. Hui, et al., HANDBOOK OF FRUIT AND
 2     VEGETABLE FLAVORS 693 (2010).
 3
             56.     That is, as a matter of food chemistry, there is no such flavor as “strawberry” or
 4
       the like. Rather, there is a ratio between acids and sugars that is consistent with what the human
 5
       tongue senses and understands as the flavor “strawberry,” and that is naturally found in
 6

 7     strawberries. See, e.g., Robert Walker and Franco Famiani, “Organic Acids in Fruits:

 8     Metabolism, Functions, and Contents,” ch. 8 in 45 H ORTICULTURAL REVIEWS 371 (2018).

 9           57.     Malic acid is found in various concentrations in almost all fruits. It is associated
10
       with two of the five primary taste sensations—sweetness and sourness—that are the main taste
11
       sensations of the Products. See id.
12
             58.     By changing the ratio between sugars and acids through the addition of malic acid
13
       in foods and beverages, a manufacturer is enabled to create from scratch or simulate a “flavor”
14

15     such as strawberry, by replicating the sugar/acid ratio present in strawberries in nature.

16           59.     By adding malic acid to a food or beverage, the manufacturer is also enabled to
17     creates tastes that resemble or reinforce the characterizing fruit flavor of the food product by
18
       providing different sweet and sour notes or “perceptions” to a flavor. A food manufacturer, for
19
       example, can use different acids (in various concentrations) to create the perception of a sweet
20
       and sour taste akin to that of vinegar by using acetic acid; to that of cream or milk by using lactic
21

22     acid; to that of lemons by using citric acid; and to that of wine by using tartaric acid. Malic acid

23     gives foods a mellower, “fruitier” sweet and sour taste reminiscent of apples. See, e.g.,

24     Reineccius, supra.
25           60.     That is, by increasing malic acid in a food formulation (often in combination with
26
       other acidulants such as citric and tartaric acids), manufacturers are enabled to push the flavor
27
       notes of a fruit flavor away from the vinegary sourness achieved by the use of acetic acid and
28
                                                       -15-
                                  SECOND AMENDED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
      Case 3:24-cv-06776-MMC           Document 52         Filed 05/12/25      Page 16 of 32



 1     towards the mellower sourness achieved by the use of malic acid, or to undercut the tanginess
 2     of citric acid. See, e.g., Reineccius, supra. This can increase the food product’s commercial
 3
       acceptability by creating tastes that resemble, but are not exactly like, the natural flavors found
 4
       in fruits.
 5
              61.    Federal regulations promulgated pursuant to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
 6

 7     (“FDCA”) require that a food’s label accurately describe the nature of the food product and its

 8     characterizing flavors. 21 C.F.R. § 102.5(a).

 9             62.   Artificial flavor is defined as “any substance, the function of which is to impart
10
       flavor, which is not derived from a spice, fruit or fruit juice, vegetable or vegetable juice, edible
11
       yeast, herb, bark, bud, root, leaf or similar plant material, meat, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy
12
       products, or fermentation products thereof.” 21 C.F.R § 101.22(a)(1).
13
               63.   Natural flavor is defined as “essential oil, oleoresin, essence or extractive, protein
14

15     hydrolysate, distillate, or any product of roasting, heating or enzymolysis, which contains the

16     flavoring constituents” from fruits or vegetables, “whose significant function in food is flavoring
17     rather than nutritional.” 21 C.F.R § 101.22(a)(3).
18
               64.   Any recognizable primary flavor identified directly or indirectly on the front label
19
